M1-01-SCHEMACEE.13:
## The income statement layout, in vertical form

The income statement prescribed by the Italian Civil Code (art. 2425) doesn't list items at random:
it groups them into classes, and the first thing a statutory (CEE) model must do is add them up in the right
order. Below you'll find a raw list of items, as they might arrive from an
accounting system: not yet in the layout, but already labelled with their class.

**Class A — Value of production**: revenue and income the income statement recognises
as the period's production. **Class B — Costs of production**: everything it cost
to produce it. The **Class** column tells you, row by row, where each item goes: A items
come first, B items right after, in the same order you see them in the table.

This level builds only the two totals and their difference — but it's the first brick:
"A) Value of production" and "B) Costs of production" will be the base for the
reclassifications, EBITDA and the three linked statements you'll see later in this module.
If these two numbers aren't solid, nothing that comes after is.
M1-01-SCHEMACEE.19: Difference between value and costs of production (A-B)
M1-01-SCHEMACEE.20: SUM({rangeA}): add up only the rows labelled "A" in the Class column.
M1-01-SCHEMACEE.21: SUM({rangeB}): add up only the rows labelled "B" in the Class column.
M1-01-SCHEMACEE.22: =C{R1}-C{R2}: the difference between the two totals you've already written above, no new number.
M1-01-SCHEMACEE.title: Italian statutory income statement
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.2: In B12 compute Value Added: (Revenue + Change in inventory) minus the sum of "external" costs — Raw materials (B6), Services (B7) and Use of third-party assets (B8). These are what the company buys from outside: what it produces with its own internal resources — personnel — is deliberately left out of this first calculation.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.3: In B13 compute the MOL (Margine Operativo Lordo, the EBITDA of this reclassified layout): start from the Value Added you already calculated in B12 and subtract Personnel costs (B9). Don't add everything up again from scratch — Value Added is already a solid number, use it as it is.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.4: In B23 compute the Contribution margin, using the alternative view below (rows 18-20), NOT the data in the value-added table above: Revenue (B18) minus Variable costs (B19). The raw materials/services/third-party asset costs of the first table have nothing to do with it — they're two different layouts, with different cost data, even though the starting revenue is the same number in both.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.5:
## Two readings of the same income statement

The income statement below is already classified: nothing to reorder, you did that in the previous
level. Here the job is different: the same income statement can be read in two different ways,
for two different purposes.

**Layout A — value added and MOL** (rows 4-9): groups costs by **nature**, i.e. by what they
are — raw materials, services, rents, personnel. It's the layout you see in published accounts.
**Value Added** is what's left of revenue after paying for everything bought
from outside (the "external" costs); **MOL** (EBITDA) is what's left after paying personnel too.

**Layout B — contribution margin** (rows 18-20): groups the SAME revenue by cost
**behaviour** — variable (grows with the volume produced/sold) or fixed (doesn't depend
on volume). These are different cost data from Layout A, generated for a different analysis:
it isn't the same breakdown read again, it's an alternative analytical cut on the same business.
The only number the two layouts share is revenue — Revenue appears identical in
both tables on purpose, to show you the starting base is the same.

**Careful**: MOL (Layout A) and Contribution margin (Layout B) are not the same measure
and have no reason to match. If they look like unrelated numbers, that's because they are: two
different readings, not two ways of double-checking the same sum.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.18: Alternative view — variable and fixed costs
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.25: =B4+B5-B6-B7-B8 : revenue plus change in inventory, minus the three "external" costs.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.26: =B12-B9 : the Value Added you've already written, minus personnel costs.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.27: =B18-B19 : Revenue from the second table minus Variable costs, not the data from the first.
M1-02-RICLASSIFICAZIONE.title: Value-added and contribution-margin reclassification
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.2: In B10 compute the prepaid expense: the part of the premium (B4) already paid but belonging to the year after 31/12 of the payment year (B8). The policy covers B5 to B7: the future portion is the share of those days that falls AFTER B8. Formula: premium × (days from B8 to B7) / (total days of the policy, from B5 to B7). Use direct subtraction between the date cells, never a number of days typed by hand.
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.3: In B19 compute the accrued expense: the part of the annual cost (B14) already accrued between the start of the service (B15) and 31/12 of the current year (B17), but not yet invoiced — no accounting document exists yet, that's exactly what an accrual is. Formula: annual cost × (days accrued, from B15 to B17) / (total days of the accrual period, from B15 to B16 — 365 or 366 depending on the year, never a number typed by hand).
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.4:
## Accruals and prepayments: when cash and accrual don't match

Correct accounts don't record costs (and revenue) when cash moves, but when 
they BELONG to the period (the accrual principle). When the two don't coincide, you need year-end
adjustments: **prepayment** and **accrual** are the two faces of the same problem, in opposite
directions.

- **Prepaid expense** — cash has ALREADY moved (a cost was paid in full), but
  part of that cost belongs to a FUTURE year. It's deferred forward: a cost
  held in suspense, not yet attributable.
- **Accrued expense** — the cost has ALREADY been incurred (a service was provided), but cash
  hasn't moved yet: no invoice has arrived. The cost is recognised anyway, for
  the part that's already economically "consumed".

**Scenario 1.** On {giorno1}/{mese1}/{anno1} an insurance premium of € {p3} was paid in full, covering {mesiPolizza} months of policy from that date. At 31/12 of the same year, the part of the premium covering the policy months of the following year is a prepaid expense: cost already paid, future period.

**Scenario 2.** On {giorno2}/{mese2}/{anno2} a service (a service contract) started, whose annual cost is € {p8}. At 31/12 the service is still in progress and no invoice has arrived yet: the share of cost already accrued up to that date is an accrued expense: cost already incurred,
cash not yet moved.
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.6: SCENARIO 1 — Prepaid expense: premium paid in full, future period
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.12: Prepaid expense — portion belonging to the following year (€)
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.13: SCENARIO 2 — Accrued expense: cost already incurred, cash not yet moved
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.16: End of the accrual period (12 months later)
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.18: Accrued expense — cost incurred not yet invoiced (€)
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.19: Prepaid expense: =B4*(B7-B8)/(B7-B5). The part of the policy falling after B8, over the total days between B5 and B7.
M1-03-RATEIRISCONTI.20: Accrued expense: =B14*(B17-B15)/(B16-B15). The days already accrued between B15 and B17, over the total period between B15 and B16.

M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.2: In B{TFR_FIN_ROW} compute the "Closing TFR": start from the opening TFR (B{TFR_INIZ_ROW}), add the year's provision (B{TFR_ACC_ROW}, it increases the fund) and subtract the uses/advances paid out during the year (B{TFR_UTIL_ROW}, they reduce the fund because they're outflows already paid to employees).
M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.3: In B{FONDO_FIN_ROW} compute the "Closing provision for risks and charges" with the same logic: opening balance (B{FONDO_INIZ_ROW}) plus provision (B{FONDO_ACC_ROW}) minus uses (B{FONDO_UTIL_ROW}). Here too the use is an outflow: it's subtracted, not added.
M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.4:
## A provision isn't a number, it's a movement

TFR (the Italian employee severance fund) and provisions for risks and charges appear in the balance sheet as a single balance, but behind them there's
always the same "cascade" (rollforward), the same one you'll build every
schedule of this module on:

**opening balance + provision for the year - uses/payments in the year = closing balance**

The provision is a cost of the year that **increases** the fund — it's added. Uses
are amounts already paid (a TFR advance paid out, a risk that materialised
and was settled) — they're an outflow, and they **reduce** the fund: they're subtracted. Flipping
this sign is the easiest mistake to make on this item, so reread it before
writing the formula.

Below you'll find two independent schedules, same structure: the **TFR** ({p0}
opening balance) and the **Provision for risks and charges** ({p1} opening balance).
Complete both closing balances.

It isn't a textbook detail: in the bridge from enterprise value (EV) to equity, TFR and risk
provisions are among the Italian items treated as debt ("debt-like items") — but
that's for a later module. Here the rollforward mechanics are enough.
M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.5: Risk provisions and TFR — movements in the year
M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.15: =B{FONDO_INIZ_ROW}+B{FONDO_ACC_ROW}-B{FONDO_UTIL_ROW}: same cascade as the TFR, different data.
M1-04-FONDIRISCHI.title: Risk provisions and TFR: the rollforward schedule
M1-05-RIMANENZE.2: In B{R_CMP} compute the weighted average unit cost of the purchased lots: weight each price by the quantity of its own lot (the simple average of the prices isn't enough, a bigger lot must count more), then divide by the total quantity purchased. A single function does the weighting in one go: SUMPRODUCT.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.3: In B{R_VAL} compute the value of closing inventory: multiply the weighted average unit cost you just calculated by the quantity left in stock at the end of the period (B{GIACENZA_ROW}).
M1-05-RIMANENZE.4: In B{R_VAR} compute the change in inventory that goes into the income statement: closing inventory minus opening inventory. If the warehouse grew in the period the result is positive (more was produced than sold), if it fell the result is negative: the sign isn't corrected by hand, it comes from the two numbers.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.5:
## Inventory: what's left in the warehouse is worth how much

During the period you bought the same goods in several lots, at different prices. At the end of the period
{p0} kg remain in the warehouse, out of a total of {p1} kg purchased: the rest has already been
sold or used. How much, in euros, are the remaining kg worth?

You can't use the price of a single lot: each one weighs by its own quantity. The method is
**weighted average cost**: the average of the prices, weighted by the quantity of each lot
instead of by the number of lots. (FIFO and LIFO exist too, but they require tracking which
specific lot was used first — a level for another time.)

Last step: inventory doesn't only sit in the balance sheet. Its **change**
— how much it grew or shrank versus the start of the period — is an income statement item
(the same "Change in inventory" you already met in class A). Here the sign
really matters: a bigger warehouse means more production than was sold.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.6: Stock ledger — purchases in the period
M1-05-RIMANENZE.10: Stock on hand at end of period (kg)
M1-05-RIMANENZE.15: SUMPRODUCT({rangeQty},{rangePrezzo})/SUM({rangeQty}): the numerator weights each price by its quantity, the denominator is the total quantity.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.16: =B{R_CMP}*B{GIACENZA_ROW}: the weighted average cost times the kg left in stock.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.17: =B{R_VAL}-B{R_INIZ}: closing inventory minus opening inventory, as they are in the cells. The sign takes care of itself.
M1-05-RIMANENZE.title: Inventory: weighted average cost
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.2: In {B_QUOTA} compute the capitalised share of development spending: the year's total spending ({p1}, in {B_SPESA}) times the percentage considered capitalisable under Italian GAAP (OIC) criteria ({p3}, in {B_PERC}). Reference the two cells, don't type the numbers: that share stops being a cost of the year in the income statement and becomes an intangible asset in the balance sheet.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.3: In {B_AMMORT} compute the annual amortisation of the capitalised share: divide the share you just calculated in {B_QUOTA} by the project's useful life in years ({B_VITA}). Reference the share already calculated, don't recompute it by multiplying spending by percentage again.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.4: In {B_DISTORSIONE} compute how much higher the EBITDA the company reports is compared with what it would have reported if all development spending had been expensed in the year, as a prudent Quality of Earnings view would want. Don't rebuild two EBITDAs in two separate cells and then subtract them: the difference is a single number, and it's exactly the share you capitalised above ({B_QUOTA}) — reference only that.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.5:
## Capitalising doesn't make a cost disappear, it moves it

This year a company spent money on research and development of a new product. Not all of this spending is necessarily a cost of the year: if the project meets the OIC (Italian GAAP) criteria (demonstrable technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete it, reliable future economic benefits...), the capitalisable part can be recorded as an intangible asset and amortised over the project's useful life, instead of hitting the income statement all at once in the year it was incurred.

Below you'll find the year's total spending ({p0}), the percentage the OIC criteria allow to be capitalised ({p1}) and the project's useful life ({vitaUtile} years).

**The delicate point** is the last task. Capitalising instead of expensing makes EBITDA look higher — not because the company generates more operating cash this year, but only because part of the cost has been moved below the line, into the amortisation of the coming years. An analyst assessing the quality of earnings wants to know exactly how big this distortion is: not two EBITDAs to compare, a single number that isolates it.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.11: Annual amortisation of the capitalised share, €
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.12: Effect on reported EBITDA vs full expensing, €
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.13: ={B_SPESA}*{B_PERC}: total spending times the capitalisable percentage.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.14: ={B_QUOTA}/{B_VITA}: the capitalised share divided by the years of useful life.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.15: ={B_QUOTA}: capitalising doesn't make the cost disappear, it moves it out of this year's income statement. Reported EBITDA is higher by exactly the share that wasn't expensed.
M1-06-CAPITALIZZAZIONE.title: Capitalising development costs
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.2: In {B_FCO} compute OPERATING cash flow: start from net income ({B_UN}), add the year's D&A ({B_DA} — an income statement cost that never left as cash) and subtract the change in Net Working Capital ({B_DCCN}). Watch the sign of {B_DCCN}: it's already presented as a signed number where POSITIVE means NWC increased and ABSORBED cash (that's why it's subtracted), NEGATIVE means NWC decreased and RELEASED cash (subtracting a negative gives it back).
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.3: In {B_FCI} compute cash flow from INVESTING: it's the year's capex ({B_CAPEX}), an outflow. Capex is given as a positive number, but in the cash flow statement an investment is cash going out: the formula must return the NEGATIVE of {B_CAPEX}.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.4: In {B_FCF} compute cash flow from FINANCING: the year's change in net financial debt ({B_DDEBITO} — already signed: positive if more debt was raised than repaid, negative if repayments prevailed) minus dividends paid ({B_DIV}, an outflow, always positive).
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.5: In {B_CASSAFIN} compute closing cash: opening cash ({B_CASSA0}) plus the three flows just calculated — operating ({B_FCO}), investing ({B_FCI}) and financing ({B_FCF}). Reference the three cells already calculated, don't rebuild the flows from scratch.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.6: In {B_CHECK} write the model's BALANCE CHECK: the difference between assets and liabilities of the year-end balance sheet, rebuilt through the three statements. Closing assets = closing cash ({B_CASSAFIN}) plus year-end non-cash assets ({B_ATTNONMON}, already calculated). Closing liabilities = year-end equity (opening equity {B_PN0}, plus net income {B_UN}, minus dividends paid {B_DIV}) plus year-end financial debt (opening debt {B_DEBITO0} plus its change {B_DDEBITO}). The formula is (Closing assets) - (Closing liabilities): if you've linked income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement correctly, this number must be EXACTLY zero. If it isn't zero, the model doesn't balance: the problem is almost always a flipped sign in one of the four previous tasks, not rounding.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.7: The model doesn't balance: year-end assets and liabilities don't match. Recheck the signs in the previous tasks (ΔNWC, capex, ΔDebt, dividends) before suspecting rounding.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.8:
## The three statements talk to each other, and they must balance

Income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement aren't three unrelated sheets: they're the same company seen from three angles, and they must tell a consistent story. The way to prove it is to build the cash flow statement with the **indirect method** — start from net income in the income statement and get, step by step, to year-end cash — and then check that this cash, added to the rest of the assets, makes the balance sheet balance exactly. If it doesn't balance, something in the model is broken: that's the **balance check**, the check every three-statement model must have.

Net income for the year {p0}, D&A for the year {p1}, change in Net Working Capital {p2} (positive = absorbed cash, negative = released it), capex {p3}, change in net financial debt {p4} (positive = more debt raised than repaid), dividends paid {p5}, opening cash {p6}.

For the final check you also need: year-end non-cash assets, already calculated ({p7} — net fixed assets, NWC and the rest of the assets that aren't cash), opening equity ({p8}) and opening financial debt ({p9}).

**The most delicate point**: the change in NWC and the change in debt already arrive as a single SIGNED number. NWC that increases has absorbed cash (receivables and inventory grew before customers paid): in operating cash flow it's SUBTRACTED. Debt that increases is cash received: in financing cash flow it's ADDED. Capex and dividends, instead, arrive as positive numbers representing an outflow: it's up to the formula to treat them as such.

Build the cash flow statement row by row, get to closing cash, and finish with the balance check: it must be zero. If it isn't zero, don't loosen the tolerance — go back and recheck a sign.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.9: Three statements: from the income statement to cash

M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.28: ={B_UN}+{B_DA}-{B_DCCN}: net income plus D&A (non-cash cost), minus the change in NWC (positive = absorbs cash).
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.29: =-{B_CAPEX}: capex is given positive, but in the cash flow statement it's an outflow.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.30: ={B_DDEBITO}-{B_DIV}: the change in debt (already signed) minus dividends (outflow).
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.31: ={B_CASSA0}+{B_FCO}+{B_FCI}+{B_FCF}: opening cash plus the three flows just calculated.
M1-07-TREPROSPETTI.32: =({B_CASSAFIN}+{B_ATTNONMON})-({B_PN0}+{B_UN}-{B_DIV}+{B_DEBITO0}+{B_DDEBITO}): closing assets minus closing liabilities. If it isn't zero, the wrong sign is almost always in ΔNWC, capex or ΔDebt.

M1-08-DASCHEDULE.4: In column D compute the ANNUAL depreciation of each asset with the straight-line method: the row's historical cost divided by the row's useful life. Start from D{CESPITE_ROW_FIRST} (= B{CESPITE_ROW_FIRST}/C{CESPITE_ROW_FIRST}) and drag it down to D{CESPITE_ROW_LAST}: it must stay the SAME formula, only shifted by row — if even a single cell in the middle has been touched up by hand or pasted as a value, that's where the error hides that you don't see until it's too late.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.5: In B{R_FONDO_FIN} compute the year-end ACCUMULATED depreciation: the accumulated depreciation already there at the start of the year (B{R_FONDO_INIZ}, depreciation accumulated in previous years) plus the sum of this year's depreciation you just built row by row in {rangeAmmortamenti}. Use SUM over the range, not the sum of each cell typed by hand.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.6: In B{R_VNC} compute the TOTAL net book value of the fixed assets: the sum of the historical costs of all assets ({rangeCosti}) minus the year-end accumulated depreciation just calculated (B{R_FONDO_FIN}). It's the number that ends up in the balance sheet assets.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.7:
## D&A isn't a number, it's a register

In M1-07 the year's D&A arrived as a single aggregated number: handy for linking the three statements, but that's not how it's really born. It comes from an **asset register**: a list of assets, each with its own historical cost and its own useful life, each with its own annual depreciation charge — which are then added up.

This year's fixed assets have {p0} items:
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.9:
**Straight-line method** (the most common, and the only one you'll see in this level): an asset's annual depreciation charge is simply its historical cost divided by its useful life in years. Each asset has its own charge, calculated with the exact same formula — only the row numbers change.

Accumulated depreciation doesn't restart from zero every year: there's already a balance accumulated in previous years, {p0}, to which the year's charge just built row by row is added. Year-end accumulated depreciation, subtracted from the total historical cost of the fixed assets, gives the **net book value**: how much the assets you own are still worth in the accounts.

Build the annual depreciation column, then the accumulated depreciation, then the total net book value — in this order, because each relies on the previous one.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.15: Accumulated depreciation and net book value
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.19: =B{CESPITE_ROW_FIRST}/C{CESPITE_ROW_FIRST}: historical cost divided by useful life. Drag it down to D{CESPITE_ROW_LAST} without touching it again.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.20: If a cell in the middle shows a number you don't trust, check its formula with F2: that's where the manual touch-up hides.
M1-08-DASCHEDULE.21: =B{R_FONDO_INIZ}+SUM({rangeAmmortamenti}): opening accumulated depreciation plus the sum of the year's charges.

M1-09-IMPOSTE.2: In {B_IMPCORR} compute the year's CURRENT TAXES: start from profit before tax ({B_UAI}), add the permanent upward adjustment ({B_VAR} — a cost already expensed in the accounts that the tax authority will never recognise) and the temporary difference deductible in the future ({B_DTD} — e.g. a risk provision, which is taxed today and will only be deductible when the provision is used). That gives you the taxable income: multiply it by the IRES rate ({B_ALIQ}).
M1-09-IMPOSTE.3: In {B_DTA} compute the DEFERRED TAX ASSETS (DTA) generated this year: the temporary difference deductible in the future ({B_DTD}) times the IRES rate ({B_ALIQ}). WATCH the sign: this is NOT an extra cost. It's a tax CREDIT — income that accrues today because in future years, when the risk provision is used, you'll pay less tax than current taxes alone. It reduces (not increases) the year's total tax charge, which you'll compute in the next task.
M1-09-IMPOSTE.4: In {B_IMPTOT} compute the year's TOTAL TAXES, the ones that go to the income statement: current taxes ({B_IMPCORR}) MINUS deferred tax assets ({B_DTA}). Deferred tax assets are income that reduces the total tax charge: they're subtracted, not added.
M1-09-IMPOSTE.5:
## Accounting profit and taxable income are not the same thing

**Stated simplification**: here you only compute IRES (Italian corporate income tax), at the real 24% rate. IRAP (regional tax) stays out — it has a different tax base (it includes labour costs) and isn't the point of this level.

The profit before tax shown in the accounts is almost never the figure on which tax is calculated. This year there are two differences between the two worlds:

- a **permanent upward adjustment** of {p0}: a cost already expensed in the accounts that the tax authority will never recognise (for example a non-deductible share of entertainment expenses). Being permanent, it doesn't generate deferred tax assets;
- a **temporary difference deductible in the future** of {p1}: the classic example is a risk provision, already inside accounting profit, which is taxed today but will only be deductible in the year the provision is actually used.

This year the tax authority treats both items the same way: BOTH are added to profit before tax to form the taxable income on which current taxes are calculated. The difference between them is what happens AFTERWARDS: only the second will reverse in a future year, and that future reversal generates a tax credit today — deferred tax assets (DTA).

**The most delicate point**: deferred tax assets are NOT an extra cost. They're income — a receivable from the tax authority that reduces the year's total tax charge, not increases it.

The year's data: profit before tax {p2}, upward adjustment {p3}, temporary difference deductible in the future {p4}, IRES rate {p5}.
M1-09-IMPOSTE.6: Current taxes and deferred tax assets (DTA)
M1-09-IMPOSTE.10: Temporary difference deductible in the future (risk provision), €
M1-09-IMPOSTE.13: Deferred tax assets (DTA) generated in the year, €
M1-09-IMPOSTE.14: Total tax charge for the year (income statement), €
M1-09-IMPOSTE.15: =({B_UAI}+{B_VAR}+{B_DTD})*{B_ALIQ}: profit before tax plus upward adjustment plus deductible temporary difference is the taxable income; multiply it by the rate.
M1-09-IMPOSTE.16: ={B_DTD}*{B_ALIQ}: the deductible temporary difference times the IRES rate. It's a credit, not a cost.
M1-09-IMPOSTE.17: ={B_IMPCORR}-{B_DTA}: current taxes minus deferred tax assets, which reduce the total charge.

M1-10-IFRS16.2: In {B_PASSIVITA} the initial lease liability: the present value of the future lease payments (paid at year end), discounted at the incremental borrowing rate. It's also the initial value of the right-of-use asset.

M1-10-IFRS16.4: In {B_INTERESSI} the first year's interest on the lease liability.
M1-10-IFRS16.5: In {B_EFFETTO_EBITDA} how much EBITDA rises compared with when the lease payment was an operating cost.

M1-10-IFRS16.7:
## The operating lease comes onto the balance sheet, and EBITDA benefits

Before IFRS 16 an operating lease payment was a cost in the income statement, above the EBITDA line. With IFRS 16 the company records a **financial liability** equal to the present value of the future lease payments and a **right-of-use asset** of the same amount. The lease payment disappears from operating costs and in its place come depreciation of the right-of-use asset and interest on the liability, **both below the EBITDA line**.

Contract: annual payment {p0} paid at year end, remaining term {durata} years, incremental borrowing rate {p2}.

Two effects to see with your own numbers: EBITDA improves without a single extra euro of cash coming in, and in the first year profit gets worse, because interest weighs more when the debt is still entirely outstanding. That's why an analyst compares the EBITDA of IFRS 16 and non-IFRS 16 companies only after adjusting it.

M1-11-STOCKCOMP.2: In {B_COSTO} compute the ANNUAL COST of the stock option plan: the total fair value granted ({B_FV}) divided by the vesting years ({B_VEST}). It's the straight-line share that vests each year: the cost of the plan is never a cash outflow, but it's still an income statement cost, spread over the years in which the employee 'earns' the right to the options.
M1-11-STOCKCOMP.3: In {B_EPSBASE} compute BASIC EPS (earnings per share): net income for the year ({B_UN}) divided by the ordinary shares actually outstanding ({B_AZBASE}). It's the "historical" EPS, read without considering any dilutive effect.
M1-11-STOCKCOMP.4: In {B_EPSDIL} compute DILUTED EPS: same net income ({B_UN}) as the previous task, but in the denominator add to the ordinary shares ({B_AZBASE}) the potential shares from the options if exercised ({B_AZPOT}) — given here already as a net number of additional shares, without applying the treasury stock method (stated simplification: that mechanism is for a future module). The same profit divided by MORE shares can only give a result lower than or equal to basic EPS: if your diluted EPS comes out higher than basic, the denominator is wrong, not the sign.
M1-11-STOCKCOMP.5:
## Stock comp: a cost without cash, and the shares that come from it

A stock option plan granted to employees has a total fair value, estimated at grant date, and vests on a straight-line basis over a number of years. Even though no cash leaves until the options are exercised, that fair value IS a cost: each vesting year absorbs a share of it in the income statement. It's the same accrual principle as accruals and prepayments, applied to a non-cash item.

Total fair value of the plan granted: {p0}. Vesting years: {p1}.
Net income for the year: {p2}. Ordinary shares outstanding: {p3}. Potential shares from the options, if exercised: {p4}.

**Why two EPS figures.** Basic EPS tells you earnings per share with the shares that exist TODAY. Diluted EPS tells the same story assuming all the granted options are exercised: same net income, but divided by MORE shares. The result is always lower than or equal to basic EPS — never the other way round — because adding shares to the denominator can't raise a ratio with the same numerator. If an analyst looks only at the basic EPS of a company that has granted lots of stock options, they're looking at a better number than the one shareholders will really see once the options are exercised.

**Stated simplification**: the potential shares below are already the net number of additional shares to add (the options are assumed to be fully exercisable and "in the money"). The full calculation would use the treasury stock method — the cash received from exercising the options buys back shares on the market, reducing net dilution — but that mechanism is for a future module: here the point is to understand the DIRECTION of the effect, not its exact calculation.

M1-12-MINORITIES.2: In {A_QUOTA_TERZI} compute the share of profit attributable to MINORITY shareholders (minority interest) in the subsidiary. The subsidiary is consolidated at 100% ({A_UTILE_CTRL} is already its full profit), but the group only owns {A_PCT_GRUPPO}: the share belonging to whoever owns the rest — the minorities — is the subsidiary's profit times (1 - group percentage).
M1-12-MINORITIES.3: In {A_QUOTA_GRUPPO} compute the profit attributable to the GROUP: total consolidated profit ({A_UTILE_CONS}, which already includes the subsidiary at 100%) minus the minority share just calculated ({A_QUOTA_TERZI}). That's how full consolidation "takes away" the minorities' slice after adding everything up.
M1-12-MINORITIES.4: In {B_CARICO_FIN} compute the CLOSING carrying value of the investment with the equity method. This associate is NOT controlled ({B_PCT_GRUPPO}, below the control threshold) and so is NEVER consolidated line by line: it's carried only as the value of the investment, which is updated like this: opening carrying value ({B_CARICO0}) PLUS the group's share of profit earned (the associate's profit {B_UTILE_PART} times {B_PCT_GRUPPO} — the carrying value RISES even though no cash has arrived) MINUS dividends received in the year ({B_DIVIDENDI} — a dividend here is a partial return of the investment, not income in the income statement, so the carrying value FALLS).
M1-12-MINORITIES.5:
## Two different situations, not to be confused

This level puts side by side two consolidation mechanics that sound alike — both talk about "how much I own" — but are conceptually opposite:

**Scenario A — Subsidiary (full consolidation).** The group CONTROLS it, so it consolidates it at 100%: every revenue and cost of the subsidiary goes into the group accounts in full, as if it were its own. But if the group doesn't own 100% of it, part of that profit belongs to whoever owns the rest — the **minorities** (minority interest). The group consolidates everything and THEN takes away the minorities' slice.

**Scenario B — Associate (equity method).** The group does NOT control it (the stake owned is below the control threshold): it NEVER consolidates it line by line. In the accounts it appears as a single line — the value of the investment — which is updated every year based on how much the associate earns and how much it distributes.

**Scenario A.** The subsidiary made a profit of {p0} (already at 100%, that's how it's consolidated). The group owns {p1} of it; the rest belongs to minorities. The group's total consolidated profit, which already includes the subsidiary's entire profit, is {p2}.

**Scenario B.** The opening carrying value of the investment is {p3}. The group owns {p4} of it — below the control threshold. In the year the associate made a profit of {p5} and paid dividends of {p6}, received by the group.

**The most delicate point of Scenario B**: under the equity method, the share of profit earned RAISES the carrying value of the investment (the group has become richer, even though it hasn't seen an extra euro of cash), while dividends received LOWER the carrying value — they're treated as a return of investment, money coming back out of what was already inside the investment, not as income in the income statement. It's the opposite of how you'd treat a dividend received from any ordinary investment, and that's exactly why it needs to be learned carefully.
